title: Fourth Word Comparison On The Necessity Of The Prescribed Prayers

questions.question: What main lesson does the story try to teach about the daily prayers?
questions.answer: It teaches that the daily prayers are extremely valuable, easy to gain compared to their reward, and very foolish to neglect.

questions.question: In the story, what did the ruler give to each servant before sending them away?
questions.answer: He gave each one twenty-four gold coins.

questions.question: Where were the two servants sent to go?
questions.answer: They were sent to settle on one of the ruler’s rich estates far away.

questions.question: About how far away was that place?
questions.answer: It was two months away.

questions.question: What were they told to use the money for?
questions.answer: They were told to buy travel fare and whatever they would need for their home there.

questions.question: What transportation choices were available on the way?
questions.answer: There were land vehicles, a train, boats, and airplanes.

questions.question: What decided which kind of transportation they could use?
questions.answer: It depended on how much money they still had.

questions.question: How did the fortunate servant use his money on the way to the station?
questions.answer: He spent only a small part of it and used some of it in a way that brought great profit.

questions.question: What happened to the fortunate servant’s wealth because of that good use?
questions.answer: It grew many times over.

questions.question: How did the other servant behave with his money?
questions.answer: He wasted almost all of it on gambling and entertainment.

questions.question: How much money did the careless servant have left at the end?
questions.answer: He had only one gold coin left.

questions.question: What advice did the first servant give his friend about that last coin?
questions.answer: He told him to use it for a ticket so he would not have to make the hard journey on foot.

questions.question: What problems would come if the careless servant did not buy the ticket?
questions.answer: He would have to travel alone, hungry, and through a desert for a very long time.

questions.question: What hope did the friend mention about the master’s kindness?
questions.answer: He said the master might forgive him and even let him ride on an airplane.

questions.question: Why is the last coin compared to a key?
questions.answer: Because using it the right way would open the way to much greater benefit.

questions.question: What does the passage say about a person who still refuses to spend that last coin wisely?
questions.answer: It says such a person would be acting in a very foolish, harmful, and senseless way.

questions.question: What idea is stressed at the very beginning of this passage about the prescribed prayers?
questions.answer: They are described as a central support of religion.

questions.question: Why does the passage use a comparison story?
questions.answer: It uses a simple example to help the reader clearly see the value of prayer and the danger of neglecting it.

questions.question: Who sent the two servants on their journey?
questions.answer: A powerful ruler sent them.

questions.question: What instruction did the ruler give besides paying for travel?
questions.answer: He told them to get what they would need for their future home.

questions.question: How far was the station from the farm?
questions.answer: It was one day away from the farm.

questions.question: What does the many transportation options show about the journey?
questions.answer: It shows that there were easier ways to arrive if a person used his money wisely.

questions.question: What good quality is seen in the first servant’s spending?
questions.answer: He was careful, thoughtful, and responsible.

questions.question: Besides careful spending, what else did the first servant do on the way?
questions.answer: He made a profitable deal or effort that pleased his master.

questions.question: How is the second servant described in character?
questions.answer: He is shown as lazy, unlucky, and careless.

questions.question: What does spending almost everything on games and fun show about his priorities?
questions.answer: It shows he cared more about short pleasure than his real goal.

questions.question: What practical reason did the friend give for buying the ticket?
questions.answer: Without it, the journey would be long, exhausting, and hungry.

questions.question: What hopeful reason did the friend add after that?
questions.answer: The master might show mercy and make the trip much easier.

questions.question: What does the desert in the story help the reader imagine?
questions.answer: It helps the reader picture hardship, loneliness, and suffering.

questions.question: Why is refusing to buy the ticket called stubbornness?
questions.answer: Because the right choice is obvious, yet the person refuses it anyway.

questions.question: What overall judgment does the passage make about trading lasting benefit for brief enjoyment?
questions.answer: It presents that choice as deeply unreasonable and damaging.

questions.question: What two things about the prescribed prayers does the passage especially want the reader to understand?
questions.answer: Their great worth and the serious foolishness of leaving them.

questions.question: According to the passage, is gaining the benefit of prayer presented as costly or low-cost?
questions.answer: It is presented as requiring very little cost.

questions.question: In the story, why were the servants given money before the journey?
questions.answer: So they could pay for travel and prepare for living in their destination.

questions.question: What happened when the first servant spent a little money in the right way?
questions.answer: It brought a huge increase in what he had.

questions.question: What does this result suggest about wise sacrifice?
questions.answer: Giving up a little in the right place can bring a much greater return.

questions.question: How did the second servant’s choices hurt his future?
questions.answer: He used up almost everything for temporary fun and left himself unprepared.

questions.question: Why was having only one coin left still important?
questions.answer: Because that one coin could still save him from a painful journey.

questions.question: What does the friend’s advice show about true friendship?
questions.answer: A true friend warns, guides, and wants good for the other person.

questions.question: What kind of journey would the servant face if he ignored the advice?
questions.answer: He would face a long, lonely, hungry trip across harsh land.

questions.question: What contrast is built between the ticket and sinful pleasure?
questions.answer: The ticket leads to safety and gain, while sinful pleasure gives only brief enjoyment and later loss.

questions.question: Why does the passage mention the master’s mercy?
questions.answer: To show that obedience can open the door to kindness beyond what a person deserves.

questions.question: If a person understands the story correctly, what choice should seem obvious?
questions.answer: He should use what remains for the ticket, not waste it on wrongdoing.

questions.question: How does the passage combine logic and warning?
questions.answer: It explains the sensible choice clearly and warns about the harm of rejecting it.

questions.question: What is the strongest message of the whole comparison?
questions.answer: A small effort for an important goal is wise, but neglecting that goal for passing pleasure is a serious mistake.

questions.question: What statement at the start shows the importance of prayer in a Muslim’s life?
questions.answer: Prayer is presented as one of the main supports of the religion.

questions.question: How certain does the passage say this matter is?
questions.answer: It says it should be as clear as a basic math truth.

questions.question: What was the ruler’s relationship to the two men in the story?
questions.answer: They were his servants under his command.

questions.question: What does sending them to a rich estate suggest about the destination?
questions.answer: It suggests the place was valuable and worth preparing for.

questions.question: Why was it important not to waste the money before reaching the station?
questions.answer: Because they still needed resources to continue the journey properly.

questions.question: What happened to the servant who acted wisely even before reaching the station?
questions.answer: He gained great benefit and increased his means.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the servant who wasted his money?
questions.answer: He is shown as idle and unfortunate.

questions.question: On what things did he waste most of his money?
questions.answer: He wasted it on gambling and entertainment.

questions.question: What was the friend trying to protect him from by telling him to buy the ticket?
questions.answer: He was trying to protect him from hardship, hunger, and a long difficult walk.

questions.question: What does the mention of an airplane add to the comparison?
questions.answer: It shows that using even a little money rightly can lead to a much easier and faster outcome.

questions.question: Which is greater in the story: the cost of the ticket or the value it can unlock?
questions.answer: The value it can unlock is far greater than its cost.

questions.question: Why is using the last coin for bad pleasure especially foolish?
questions.answer: Because it would throw away the final chance to reach safety and benefit.

questions.question: What can a reader infer about short-lived fun from this passage?
questions.answer: It can blind a person to his real needs and harm his future.

questions.question: What kind of person is being warned in this comparison?
questions.answer: A person who ignores what truly matters and wastes his chances.

questions.question: How would you sum up the message of the story in one sentence?
questions.answer: A smart person gives up a little now for a much better ending later.

questions.question: What is being compared in this passage through the story of the two servants?
questions.answer: The story compares wise attention to prayer with careless neglect of it.

questions.question: Why does the passage say the one who neglects prayer is acting badly?
questions.answer: Because he gives up something very valuable even though it asks little from him.

questions.question: How much money did each servant start with?
questions.answer: Each one started with twenty-four gold coins.

questions.question: What job were they expected to do after traveling?
questions.answer: They were expected to settle in and prepare a home on the ruler’s estate.

questions.question: What does this show about the journey?
questions.answer: It was a move toward a serious and lasting destination.

questions.question: How did the successful servant balance spending and gain?
questions.answer: He spent carefully and turned part of his effort into major profit.

questions.question: What mistake did the other servant make besides wasting money?
questions.answer: He let entertainment distract him from his real mission.

questions.question: Why did his friend speak to him after he was left with one coin?
questions.answer: Because there was still time to make one wise choice.

questions.question: What does the advice about buying a ticket teach about small acts?
questions.answer: A small act can have huge results when it is tied to an important goal.

questions.question: What is the difference between the outcomes of the two possible choices for the last coin?
questions.answer: One choice leads toward safety and arrival, while the other leads toward suffering and loss.

questions.question: What does the possibility of the master’s forgiveness add to the meaning of the story?
questions.answer: It shows that mercy may come to the one who turns in the right direction.

questions.question: Why does the passage say even the least intelligent person can understand this point?
questions.answer: Because the right choice is very plain and does not require complicated thinking.

questions.question: What human weakness is the wasteful servant mainly showing?
questions.answer: He is showing weakness in self-control and judgment.

questions.question: How does the passage treat pleasure that comes from wrongdoing?
questions.answer: It treats it as short, deceptive, and destructive in the end.

questions.question: What lesson should an 8th-grade Muslim student take from this story?
questions.answer: Do not throw away great reward for short fun; choose what helps your deen and your future.

questions.question: What role do the prescribed prayers have in religion according to the opening line?
questions.answer: They have a foundational role, like a main support holding something up.

questions.question: What three ideas does the passage promise to explain through the comparison?
questions.answer: It explains the value of prayer, the small cost of gaining its reward, and the foolishness of neglecting it.

questions.question: In the story, what does the ruler first provide the servants with?
questions.answer: He provides them with money to help them reach their destination.

questions.question: What does that gift suggest about responsibility?
questions.answer: It suggests they were given enough to act wisely and are responsible for how they use it.

questions.question: Why were different forms of travel mentioned together?
questions.answer: To show that better and easier options are open to the one who manages his means well.

questions.question: What made the first servant “fortunate” in the story?
questions.answer: He used his resources carefully and in a way that brought approval and benefit.

questions.question: What made the second servant “luckless”?
questions.answer: He was lazy and wasted his money on useless pleasures.

questions.question: Why did only one coin remain for the careless servant?
questions.answer: Because he had spent nearly everything on bad entertainment.

questions.question: What wise use of the final coin was suggested?
questions.answer: It should be spent on a ticket for the journey.

questions.question: How is the ticket described in terms of value?
questions.answer: It is treated like something that opens the door to a treasure.

questions.question: What would happen if that coin were used for vice instead?
questions.answer: The servant would lose his chance for easier travel and fall into hardship.

questions.question: What physical difficulties are named if he travels without the ticket?
questions.answer: He would have to walk a very long distance and suffer hunger.

questions.question: What emotional or moral problem is also shown in refusing the ticket?
questions.answer: It shows stubbornness and poor judgment.

questions.question: How does the master’s possible kindness make the servant’s refusal even worse?
questions.answer: Because help and forgiveness might still be available, yet he would still be turning away from them.

questions.question: What kind of reader response does the final question in the passage try to create?
questions.answer: It pushes the reader to admit that the foolish choice is obviously wrong.

questions.question: What is the central message of the whole passage?
questions.answer: Choosing brief sinful enjoyment over a small effort for a great reward is a reckless mistake.
